questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
I come from a university where undergraduate teaching is primarily conducted in Danish. We had one course in the third semester worth 5 ECTS credits that was taught in English, but that was the only one. The students at Maastricht University were fluent in legal English, which meant that linguistically I was far behind my fellow students. Fortunately, I gradually caught up with the language, but this only happened after four months, by which point I had already completed my courses.
Both the level of language and the academic level were extremely high. Not only were we, as exchange students, expected to have the same foundational knowledge as the other ELS (European Law Students), but it was also difficult to adapt to their teaching format. Maastricht University operates a period system where teaching is divided into two periods. Each period ended with a two-hour exam. Some exams were open-book, while others were closed-book. As a Danish student, I had never taken an exam without notes before. In the second period alone, I had three closed-book exams.
During each period, we were required to submit midterms that counted toward a percentage of the final exam grade. This meant that over the course of four months, I effectively had to do an exam ten times. These midterms could take the form of debates, written assignments, presentations, or a mock trial. I can understand the advantages of making teaching more dynamic in this way, but under the conditions we were placed in, it was not possible to keep up as an exchange student.
In addition, the teaching method was based on “problem-based learning,” meaning that we had to prepare a case and complete readings for every class. This teaching style is quite similar to the Danish system, which I actually appreciated. However, many of my fellow exchange students found it overwhelming and unfamiliar. My main challenge within this system was the extremely high expectations for the level of the cases, on top of preparing for midterms, keeping up with the extensive reading across multiple courses, and simultaneously struggling with the language. Whenever I did not have scheduled teaching, I spent the rest of the day in the library studying 
The teaching structure was such that we did not really have a teacher. Instead, we had a tutor who was considered responsible for the course. One student was either appointed or volunteered to act as the “discussion leader” and manage the class. I was appointed once, which was nerve-wracking and absolutely not something I wanted, but I did it. It is an experience I can now include on my CV, but it was not something I would have chosen voluntarily during my exchange.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Don't try! Befriend other exchange students through sport or ESN. 

The environment among the regular students (ELS) was very toxic. I witnessed fellow students laughing at others and making comments such as, “How can she be 28 and so clueless?”. There was whispering in corners, and discussions during class could become uncomfortable, without any of the teachers or tutors intervening. This environment does not encourage exchange students—who already lack the same background knowledge and do not speak the language fluently—to participate in class. On the contrary, I have never participated orally so little during my entire academic career.

Don't take more than 4 courses. If the points doesn't fit, choose 4 courses with 32 point instead of 5 with 30. That was a big mistake
